prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My mother the queen is dead. My father the king is old. He fumbles his cirque of gold And dreams of a year long fled. The young men stare at my face, But cannot meet my glance— Cavan tall as a lance, Orra swift in the race. Death was ever my price, Since my maidenhood began: At the thought of a Gaelic man My heart is sister of ice. ’Tis another for whom I wait, Though I have not kissed his sword: He or none is my lord, Though our night be soon or late. The star grows great in my breast: It is crying clearly now To the star on the burnished prow Of his galley far in the West. The capes of the North are dim, And the windward beaches smoke Where the last long roller spoke The tidings it held of him. Sorrow I know he brings, Battle, despair and change,— Beauty cruel and strange, And the shed bright blood of kings. Breast, be white for his sake! Mouth, be red for the kiss! Soul, be strong for your bliss! Heart, be ready to break!

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: And, The, But

outputs.L1:
My mother, the Queen, is dead.  
My father, the King, is old;  
He fumbles with his circlet of gold  
And dreams of a year long fled.  

The young men gaze upon my face,  
Yet cannot meet my glance—  
Cavan, tall as a lance,  
Orra, swift in the race.  

Death has ever been my price  
Since first my maidenhood began;  
At the thought of a Gaelic man,  
My heart turns sister to ice.  

It is another for whom I wait,  
Though I have not kissed his sword;  
He, or none, shall be my lord,  
Whether our night come soon or late.  

The star grows bright within my breast;  
It cries out clearly now  
To the star on the burnished prow  
Of his galley far in the West.  

The capes of the North grow dim,  
And the windward beaches smoke  
Where the last long roller spoke  
The tidings it bore of him.  

Sorrow, I know, he brings—  
Battle, despair, and change;  
Beauty, cruel and strange,  
And the bright spilled blood of kings.  

Breast, be white for his sake!  
Mouth, be red for the kiss!  
Soul, be strong for your bliss!  
Heart, be ready to break!
outputs.L2:
My queenly mother has died.  
My father, the king, has grown frail with age.  
He toys uncertainly with his golden circlet  
And dreams of a year vanished long ago.  

Young men look upon my face,  
Yet they cannot hold my eyes—  
Cavan, straight and tall like a spear,  
Orra, fleetest in the running.  

Death has always been the cost of me  
Since first I came to womanhood:  
When I think of any Gaelic man,  
My heart turns cold as a sister to ice.  

It is another man I am waiting for,  
Though I have never kissed his blade.  
He alone shall be my lord, or no one shall,  
Whether our meeting comes early or late.  

A star swells bright within my breast;  
Its cry rings out plainly now  
To the star upon the polished prow  
Of his ship far away in the West.  

The northern headlands fade into shadow,  
And the beaches facing the wind are misted with spray  
Where the last great wave has broken,  
Bearing the news it carried of him.  

I know he comes bringing grief,  
War, hopelessness, and upheaval—  
A beauty fierce, pitiless, and unfamiliar,  
And the brilliant spilled blood of kings.  

Breast, be pale for his coming!  
Mouth, be crimson for his kiss!  
Soul, be steadfast for your joy!  
Heart, be prepared to shatter!
outputs.L3:
The speaker is a young woman living under the shadow of loss and change. She mourns the death of her mother, whose absence leaves an emotional emptiness at the center of her life. At the same time, she watches her father grow old and withdrawn, as though he is slowly disappearing into the memories of his own past. His connection to the present weakens, and the household seems marked by fading grief and quiet decline.

Although young men admire the speaker and are drawn to her beauty, she does not return their affection. Their attention leaves her unmoved. In particular, she remains emotionally distant from the Gaelic suitors who seek her favor. However worthy or passionate they may be, she cannot give herself to them. Her heart is withheld, not from pride alone, but because she senses that her fate lies elsewhere.

Instead, she waits for a destined man from the West. Though she has not yet met him, she already recognizes him inwardly as her true lord. Her loyalty and desire are directed toward this unknown figure, as if some deeper power has chosen him for her before his arrival. He exists first as a prophecy, a vision, or a certainty in her imagination, but he is more real to her than the men who stand before her.

The natural world seems to confirm this expectation. Omens appear in the sea and in the stars, suggesting that the awaited man is drawing near. These signs do not promise peace or simple happiness. Rather, they announce the coming of fate itself. The movements of the heavens and the restless waters seem to carry warnings of transformation, conflict, and destiny.

The speaker understands that his arrival will change everything. She anticipates not only beauty and passion, but also sorrow, battle, upheaval, and heartbreak. The man from the West will bring intensity and grandeur, yet also suffering. His coming will awaken love, but it will also disturb the world around her. In accepting him before she has even seen him, the speaker accepts the full burden of the fate he represents: desire joined with pain, splendour joined with ruin, and love inseparable from loss.
outputs.L4:
The speaker is a princess who stands at the edge of change, mourning the death of her queen-mother and watching her king-father grow old. Around her, the familiar world of the court continues: noblemen seek her hand, local suitors offer safety, rank, and tradition, and the kingdom expects her to choose a husband who will preserve the old order. Yet she refuses them all. Her grief has made her inward-looking and visionary, and she speaks in a lyrical first-person voice filled with images of darkness, blood, wind, stars, and distant horizons. These images suggest that her love is not merely a romantic preference but something foretold, something woven into fate.

Instead of accepting the men who surround her, the princess longs for a warrior who will come from the West. He is not presented as gentle or harmless. He belongs to a world of battle, movement, and upheaval, and his arrival promises danger as much as fulfillment. The symbols surrounding him are prophetic: he seems to come with storm, fire, and violence, as if his love will break open the stagnant life of the palace. The princess understands this. She does not imagine that he will bring peace or simple happiness. Rather, she welcomes the sorrow, passion, and destruction that may accompany him, because they answer something deep within her own soul.

Her desire therefore becomes more than private longing. It reflects the passing of one royal age and the approach of another. The dead queen and aging king represent a fading order, while the distant warrior embodies change, conflict, and renewal. By choosing him in her imagination before he even arrives, the princess accepts her own destiny and the transformation of the kingdom. Her love is both personal and political, both emotional and prophetic. The poem presents her longing as a force that joins grief with desire, death with renewal, and individual passion with the larger movement of history.
outputs.L5:
**And, The, But**

Small words often carry great weight. **And** connects ideas, bringing people, thoughts, and possibilities together. It suggests addition, cooperation, and continuation. With “and,” a sentence grows; a story moves forward.

**The** gives focus. It points to something specific, something known or important. Instead of speaking generally, “the” helps us identify exactly what we mean. It brings clarity and direction to language.

**But** introduces contrast. It shows that ideas can change, conflict, or surprise us. “But” reminds us that life is not always simple; there are challenges, exceptions, and different perspectives.

Together, **and**, **the**, and **but** may seem ordinary, but they shape meaning in powerful ways. They connect, define, and challenge our thoughts, proving that even the smallest words can make a big difference.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a young Celtic princess awaiting a foreign warrior-lover, with archaic diction, royal imagery, prophecy, death, battle, and tragic romance.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Princess at the Western Tower**

Lo, I have set my lamp upon the stone,  
High in the tower where sea-winds cry;  
My father’s banners, rent and lone,  
Beat at the moon’s cold eye.

The harp is hush’d in the painted hall,  
The hounds lie still by the ashen door;  
Yet I hear thy horn beyond the wall,  
O stranger from the southern shore.

They named thee foe in my father’s keep,  
They cursed thy blade at the feast of kings;  
But I beheld thee out of sleep,  
Where dream to doom the raven brings.

A seeress came with hair of snow,  
And eyes like wells where dead men gleam:  
“Daughter of crowns, thou shalt love him so  
Thy bridal bed shall be a stream.

“His helm shall shine in a field of red,  
His spear shall break where the war-hosts meet;  
Thou shalt kiss no mouth but the mouth of the dead,  
And bind no gold but about cold feet.”

Yet still I braid my hair with pearl,  
And clasp the brooch of my mother’s line;  
I am no shepherd’s trembling girl—  
The blood of queens is fire in mine.

Come over the moor where the white mists crawl,  
Come under the stars with thy sword unshorn;  
Though spears be thick by my father’s wall,  
I shall know thy tread ere morn.

The oak hath groaned in the sacred wood,  
The salmon leapt from the prophet’s pool;  
Three times the moon was stained with blood,  
And the wise men spake of a broken rule.

My brothers arm in their wolf-skin pride,  
Their shields are black with a raven’s wing;  
They laugh to think thou shalt not ride  
Alive through the gates of the high-born king.

But I have laid by my maiden veil,  
And I have loosened my girdle’s gold;  
If thou art slain in the iron hail,  
I shall not live to be bartered and sold.

For what is a crown but a circlet of thorn?  
What is a throne but a stone of tears?  
Better the breast by a spearhead torn  
Than loveless days and dishonoured years.

Hark! on the heath there riseth a roar—  
The clang of bronze, the battle-cry;  
The tide runs crimson along the shore,  
And ravens darken the morning sky.

Ride, my beloved! Ride through flame!  
Let thy bright sword make answer true;  
I shall call thee not by thy foreign name,  
But by the name my heart gave you.

If thou dost fall where the war-drums cease,  
I’ll come in white through the slaughtered men;  
I’ll lay my cheek to thy wound for peace,  
And never return to the tower again.

And when old bards by winter fire  
Sing of the maid with the golden hair,  
Say not she died of vain desire—  
Say love was king, and found her there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Yeats-inspired dramatic monologue about an Irish queen’s daughter whose mother is dead, whose father is aging, and whose heart rejects Gaelic suitors while she waits for a mysterious lord from the West.
counterfactuals.output:
I am the daughter of a queen gone down  
Under the cairn-stones and the rainy grass;  
They say her hair was like the harvest moon,  
Her voice a bell that made the wild swans pass  
Low over Innisfail. I have her ring,  
Cold on my hand, and all her silences.  
My father in the hall is withering,  
A candle baffled by the western seas.

The young men come with horses and with hounds,  
With harps that quarrel sweetly with the fire;  
They praise the red deer on the windy grounds,  
They praise old kings, and name me their desire.  
O smooth are Gaelic tongues, and brave their eyes,  
And proud the cloaks that glimmer in the rain—  
Yet when they speak, my heart, that should arise,  
Falls back like ashes into ash again.

For I have heard, beyond the crying foam,  
A horn blown once, and not by mortal breath;  
And I have seen, when evening filled the room,  
A shadow at the threshold still as death.  
He wore no badge of any clan I know,  
No brooch of Tara, and no Ulster blade;  
His cloak was dusk, his face a hidden glow,  
As if the last light loved him and obeyed.

They mock me: “Dreamer, will you wed the air?  
Will you grow old beside an empty chair?  
Take gold, take land, take children at your knee;  
No lord comes riding from the western sea.”  
But I have watched the gulls wheel white and far,  
And seen the sun sink like a burning crown;  
There is a country under evening’s star  
Where all lost queens and kings go wandering down.

Mother, if you have speech beneath the mound,  
Or if your beauty walks in some bright place,  
Send me a sign upon the salt-wind’s sound,  
A flame, a feather, or a lifted face.  
For father sleeps; the hounds no longer cry;  
The banners rot; the bards forget their lays;  
And I, who cannot love the men nearby,  
Am set apart from ordinary days.

Come, lord unknown, out of the western foam,  
Out of the rose-red islands of the blest;  
Come before age has made my heart a tomb,  
And lay your twilight hand upon my breast.  
For I was born where grief and glory meet,  
A queen’s dead daughter in a dying house;  
I will not cast my dreams at any feet,  
Nor bind my soul to an unchosen vow.

Let others take the kiss, the ring, the name,  
The fruitful field, the cradle, and the song;  
I keep a vigil at a darker flame,  
And I have waited, and will wait, too long.  
Though all the court grow grey with their disdain,  
Though winter whiten every tower above—  
My heart is westward, westward through the rain,  
And what I wait for must be more than love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical ballad in quatrains about a princess in an ancient Gaelic kingdom sensing the approach of her destined beloved by sea, mixing beauty, bloodshed, sorrow, and ecstatic anticipation.
counterfactuals.output:
The moon on Tara’s western stones  
Lay pale as milk on mail and thorn,  
When Eithne heard beneath the foam  
A horn no mortal hand had borne.  

The gulls cried out like widowed queens,  
The kelp smoked black on silver sand;  
Far off, beyond the battle-green,  
Her lover’s ship drew toward the land.  

She felt him first within her blood,  
A tide that climbed her breast and bone;  
Though crows were feeding in the mud  
Where kings had fallen for her throne.  

Her hair was red as rowan flame,  
Her gown was stitched with pearls and tears;  
She whispered once her hidden name  
To winds that had not changed in years.  

“O sea,” she sang, “you salt-dark bride,  
Bring home the heart the gods have sworn;  
Though spears have reddened every tide,  
Let joy rise naked with the morn.”  

Below, the clans with axes bright  
Stood grieving round the funeral pyre;  
Above, she burned through grief and night,  
A candle caught by starry fire.  

For she had dreamed his raven sail,  
His hand like heat upon her hand,  
His kiss that turned the war-horns frail,  
His feet made holy on the strand.  

Yet blood was on the heather still,  
And brothers slept beneath the rain;  
The harp was broken on the hill,  
Its strings all tangled up with pain.  

Still Eithne laughed, and still she wept,  
Half maiden, half enchanted sea;  
The ancient oaks around her kept  
Their dark and druid prophecy.  

Then through the mist, with dawn behind,  
A black prow split the shining foam;  
She cried aloud against the wind,  
“My sorrow ends. My love comes home.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem beginning with “My mother the queen is dead. My father the king is old.” and continue in a romantic, mythic, Celtic style with images of stars, galleys, northern capes, and doomed love.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother the queen is dead. My father the king is old.  
The harp in the hall hangs silent, the hearth is ash and cold;  
Yet over the western water the wild white planets burn,  
And the gulls cry out at morning for ships that will not return.

I saw her once by moonrise where the blackthorn meets the foam,  
With a crown of rowan berries and eyes like the lights of home;  
Her cloak was woven twilight, her voice was rain on stone,  
And my heart went out like a falcon, and came not back alone.

We launched our galleys northward, with sails like swans in flight,  
Past Skye and the bitter skerries, past islands drowned in night;  
The stars were silver runes there, on heaven’s iron shield,  
And the wind blew cold from the capes where no green branches yield.

She stood beside the masthead, a flame the storm could spare,  
Salt on her lips like sorrow, dark waves in her hair.  
“O prince of a house that is failing, O heir to a withered throne,  
Love me only till dawn breaks—then leave me to die alone.”

But I had heard in childhood the songs of the seal-maid’s kin,  
How love is a net of starlight no mortal man may win;  
How brides of the hidden people must vanish before the sun,  
And he who follows after is lost when the tides are done.

Still north by the ghostly headlands our oars beat time with doom,  
Under the wheeling Bear-star, through leagues of green sea-gloom;  
And there at the world’s last margin, where the cliffs like giants stand,  
She kissed me once in silence and slipped from my mortal hand.

Down went the moon behind her, down went the mast and spar,  
The sea took back her daughter, the sky took back its star.  
Now I rule in a hall of echoes, with a crown of tarnished gold,  
My mother the queen lies buried. My father the king is old.

But when the winter deepens, and the northern lights are high,  
I hear her singing under the keel of the midnight sky;  
And I would trade throne and kingdom, and name and blood and breath,  
For one more sail beyond the cape, and one more kiss in death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an archaic dramatic poem from the perspective of a royal maiden who knows love will bring death and political upheaval, but still prepares herself for the arrival of her true lord.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Maiden in the Tower**

Lo, bid the torches lower flame,  
And draw the purple curtain wide;  
For ere the cock hath cried his name,  
My lord shall ride—my lord shall ride.

I know the stars have writ in fire  
What doom beneath his banner goes;  
I know my father’s halls aspire  
To ash, and blood shall drown the rose.

The council mutters in the stone,  
The priests have veiled the altar’s face;  
They say, “O child, remain alone,  
And save thy sire’s ancient race.”

They bring me treaties, seals, and rings,  
Cold parchments bound with golden thread;  
They speak of peace with neighboring kings—  
Yet all their peace is with the dead.

For love, that sweet and sovereign blade,  
Hath cleft the helm of policy;  
And I, a king’s unbartered maid,  
Have heard my fate and answer: Yea.

Yea, though his coming shake the gate,  
Though trumpet shriek and charger foam;  
Yea, though he bear the brand of fate,  
And bring no bridal-gift but doom.

Let matrons comb my raven hair,  
And set therein the pearls of state;  
Let scarlet robes my bosom bear,  
As though I went to wed—not hate.

Bring forth the crown I may not keep,  
The girdle wrought in elder wars;  
And from the chapel, dark with sleep,  
The veil embroidered thick with stars.

For I would meet him as a queen,  
Though queens be dust ere moonset wanes;  
With lips unblanched, with brow serene,  
Though ruin rattles at my chains.

O father, sleep behind thy doors;  
Dream yet thy sceptre shall endure.  
The river creeps about thy floors;  
The torch is set; the end is sure.

O mother, in thy marble bed,  
If dead queens hear beneath the ground,  
Forgive the daughter thou hast bred  
For loving where the curse is found.

I did not seek him; nay, the skies  
Bent down and laid him in my sight:  
A storm of stars was in his eyes,  
His voice the breaking of the night.

He called me not with courtly breath,  
Nor sued me soft with minstrel’s art;  
He spake as one familiar with death:  
“Thou art the kingdom of my heart.”

Then fell the moon behind the keep,  
Then ceased the viol and the jest;  
And something ancient woke from sleep  
And laid its hand upon my breast.

Since then the lark hath sung in vain,  
The hawthorn bloomed but seemed a shroud;  
I heard, in every drop of rain,  
The marching of a buried crowd.

They say his claim is forged in blood,  
His right denied, his sword unblest;  
That if he cross the western wood,  
A thousand spears shall pierce the west.

Then let them rise. Let banners tear.  
Let brother set on brother’s brow.  
What is a throne to one despair?  
What is a realm to such a vow?

I am no dove for barter born,  
No lamb to gild a butcher’s peace;  
I am the bride of thunder sworn,  
And from my oath have no release.

Yet fear not: I do tremble still.  
My hands are cold beneath the gem.  
Love is a cup none drink at will  
But God hath filled the brim for them.

I see the scaffold in the square,  
The ravens on the windy wall;  
I see my lord’s bright loosened hair,  
Or mine—perchance—before them all.

I see the crown in pieces flung,  
The charter burned, the nobles slain;  
The old songs choked in every tongue,  
And children asking bread in vain.

And still—O Heaven, pity me!—  
I set the silver on my brow;  
For had I leave from love to flee,  
I would not take that freedom now.

Hark!—Was it hoof upon the bridge?  
Nay, but mine own heart’s furious beat.  
The dawn stands pale upon the ridge;  
The mist kneels low about his feet.

Unbar the postern. Leave me room.  
Let no man speak of flight or shame.  
Though through that door advance my doom,  
I go to meet it like a flame.

My lord, my death, my crown, my sword,  
Come forth from night and claim thine own.  
The bride is robed; the feast is stored;  
The kingdom quakes beneath the throne.

And if thy kiss be mortal sweet,  
And if our bridal-bed be stone,  
Still shall my spirit rise to meet  
Thee there, as here, thy bride alone.

For love is lordlier than kings,  
And sterner than the grave’s decree;  
It breaks the sceptres, burns the rings,  
And makes the captive soul more free.

So let the bells, though cracked, be swung;  
Let all the sleeping towers awake.  
The song for coronation sung  
Shall serve as dirge ere daybreak.

Lo, bid the torches leap in flame,  
And cast the purple curtain wide;  
For ere the sun hath crowned my shame,  
My lord shall ride—my lord shall ride.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
